summary_html: A **parent/guardian/child requests help** without a substantiated allegation. FFPSA created a federal pathway for **prevention services** to avert removal and stabilize families before a case escalates.
authority_html: - **Family First Prevention Services Act (2018)** — prevention services, kinship support; shifts upstream from removal to support

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: As applied, a statute authorizing any person to petition for visitation over a fit parent's objection violated the mother's due process right to make decisions concerning the care, custody and control of her children.
key_cases.relevance: A fit parent's own request for or refusal of services is entitled to the presumption of correctness Troxel describes.
key_cases.quote: the application of § 26.10.160(3) to Granville and her family violated her due process right to make decisions concerning the care, custody, and control of her daughters

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Because the father had consented to the initial removal and safety arrangement, no clearly established law put the caseworker on notice that her conduct violated the family's Fourth or Fourteenth Amendment rights, and qualified immunity was granted.
key_cases.relevance: It shows how a parent's request for help or agreement to a plan is later treated as consent that forfeits procedural protections.
key_cases.quote: Absent certain exigent circumstances, the state's termination of or interference with parental rights—even temporarily—requires some measure of procedural protection, like proper notice and an opportunity for a hearing.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Fourth Amendment governs a social worker's in-school interview of a child during a child-abuse investigation, requiring at a minimum reasonable suspicion of abuse, and the court affirmed denial of qualified immunity on the children's Fourth Amendment claims and on the parents' Fourteenth Amendment claims arising from a coercive in-home safety plan.
key_cases.relevance: It shows that a parent's apparent cooperation with a caseworker's plan is not voluntary consent when it is obtained under threat of removal.
key_cases.quote: a social worker must have a reasonable suspicion of child abuse before conducting an in-school interview when no other exception to the Fourth Amendment's warrant requirement applies

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Sixth Circuit affirmed summary judgment for an Ohio caseworker, holding that where parents voluntarily consent to a safety plan placing their children outside the home and never use the plan's stated mechanism to revoke that consent, no pre-removal hearing is required and there is no procedural due process violation.
key_cases.relevance: It is the counterweight to Schulkers: a parent's agreement to a plan is treated as continuing consent until the parent affirmatively revokes it, and displeasure or repeated questions do not amount to revocation.
key_cases.quote: the Smiths needed to explicitly withdraw the consent they explicitly gave, thus requiring Children's Services to either return the children or file a formal complaint against them

state_agency.name: Ohio Department of Children and Youth

mandatory_reporters: Listed professionals only — Ohio is not a universal-reporting state; any other person may report voluntarily (Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.421(A)(1)(b), (B))
Attorneys
Health care professionals (defined at Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.421(O)(2))
Practitioners of a limited branch of medicine (Ohio Rev. Code § 4731.15)
Licensed school psychologists and independent marriage and family therapists or marriage and family therapists
Coroners
School teachers, school employees and school authorities
Administrators and employees of child care centers, residential camps, child day camps and private, nonprofit therapeutic wilderness camps

Administrators and employees of certified child care agencies and other public or private children services agencies, and third parties employed by a public children services agency to assist in providing child or family related services
Peace officers
Humane society agents, dog wardens, deputy dog wardens and other appointed animal control officers
Persons, other than clerics, rendering spiritual treatment through prayer in accordance with the tenets of a well-recognized religion
Clerics and non-volunteer leaders, officials or delegates designated by a church, religious society or faith (Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.421(A)(4))
Employees of a county department of job and family services who are professionals working with children and families
Employees of entities providing home visiting services under the Help Me Grow program (Ohio Rev. Code § 5180.21)
Superintendents and regional administrators employed by the Department of Youth Services

Superintendents, board members and employees of county boards of developmental disabilities, contracted investigative agents, Department of Developmental Disabilities employees, and employees of facilities or homes providing respite care (Ohio Rev. Code § 5123.171)
Employees of entities that provide homemaker services
Employees of qualified organizations and host families (Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.90)
Foster caregivers
Persons performing the duties of an assessor under Ohio Rev. Code Chapter 3107 or 5103
Court appointed special advocates and guardians ad litem

timeline_requirements.deadline: Within 24 hours, except as provided in Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.422 or in an interagency agreement entered into under Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.428 that applies to the particular report
timeline_requirements.starts_from: Report referred to the public children services agency
timeline_requirements.consequence_of_miss: Statute sets no penalty; Ohio Rev. Code § 2151.421(G)(1) states that a failure to investigate in accordance with the county memorandum of understanding is not grounds for dismissing charges or suppressing evidence

timeline_requirements.deadline: No later than 60 days (family assessment recorded and approved)

parent_rights_at_moment: Right to refuse entry without warrant
